 artery, right vertebral artery, left common carotid artery, left internal

 proximal to the intracranial internal carotid artery bifurcation.  Injection
 of the right and left vertebral arteries reveals the presence of a focal mid
 basilar region of vasospasm.  This results in approximately 50% decrease in
 the lumen of the basilar artery for a region of approximately 4 mm.  In
 addition, three-dimensional rotational angiography again reveals the presence
 of a basilar fenestration at the vertebrobasilar junction which is free of
 aneurysmal anomaly.  Injection of the left internal carotid artery reveals
 again presence of focal spasm which involves in diffuse fashion the left M1
 segment of the intracranial distribution of the internal carotid artery.  The
 distal branches appear to be free of vasospasm.  In addition, injection of

medial history, no past surgical history, no known
drug allergies and took no medications.

ecchymoses of the face and head. She was complaining of a
headache as well as some abdominal pain and diarrhea for
several days. Her abdomen was soft but tender and she was
guaiac positive on rectal examination.

well as CT scan of the head and C-spine. A Foley catheter was
placed with a minimal amount of urine retrieved. She was noted
to have pyuria. While the CT scan of the head and C-spine
revealed no abnormalities.  Laboratory tests revealed a white
blood cell count of 43,000.  Creatinine of 3.7. INR of 1.7 and
lactate of 5.7.

The emergency department ordered a renal ultrasound at this
time to rule out an obstructive cause of anuria and a CT of
the abdomen and pelvis with PO contrast were ordered.
While awaiting the report of the CT scan however, the patient
became acutely hypoxic with oxygen saturations in the 80's and
was emergently intubated. The CT scan demonstrated thickened
small bowel, and large amount of ascites (of note, the patient
was severely hypoalbuminemic of uncertain etiology). A
surgical consult was obtained at approximately 8 p.m. to
evaluate the patient for possible ischemic bowel. The patient
was septic but the source uncertain in this patient with
pyuria. She was continued to be resuscitated and had received
approximately 7 liters of crystalloid at this time. A repeat
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast down to the
rectum now revealed stable small bowel thickening but also
thickening of the transverse colon, sigmoid and rectum. The
patient was brought to the surgical intensive care unit  and
rigid sigmoidoscopy was performed but the colon could not be
seen proximally. There was a question of whether there was
dusky discoloration at 15 cm but this was not clear.

Therefore a stat GI consult was obtained to perform a
colonoscopy and evaluate the extent of colonic involvement.
The colonoscopy demonstrated an area of 15 to 20 cm of mucosal
discoloration with more proximal mucosal edema and friability
in the splenic flexure descending colon and sigmoid,
consistent with ischemia. The terminal ileum was also
abnormal.  Based on the above as well as persistent acidosis
the patient was taken emergently to the operating room for
exploration.

The patient underwent an exploratory laparotomy. On entering
the abdomen, a large amount of ascites was discovered with
turbid fluid in the pelvis. The liver was studded with
multiple white/tan firm nodules, later confirmed to be
metastatic adenocarcinoma. While the descending colon and
proximal sigmoid were edematous with areas consistent with
ischemia, there was no full-thickness involvement. However at
the rectosigmoid junction there was an area of congested
purple appearance of the bowel that felt circumferentially
firm and worrisome for malignancy. The patient underwent a
colectomy and Hartmann's procedure and was transferred back to
the ICU on multiple pressors. She continued to have a large
fluid requirement to maintain adequate filling pressures,
cardiac index and tissue perfusion by SGO2 and received over
15 liters of crystalloid during the first 24 hours of her
admission.

By postoperative day No. 1, she was having increased peak
airway pressures above 40 cc of water as well as multiple
bladder pressure measurements over a 2 hour period, greater
than 40 cm of water. Her abdominal compartment was emergently
decompressed at the bed time with an almost immediate
improvement in hemodynamics. Her abdomen was closed with
[**Location (un) 5701**] bag technique. Unfortunately these improvements were
short lived and she progressively deteriorated developing
refractory hypotension and acidosis requiring maximal amounts
of vasopressor and Levophed to maintain adequate blood
pressure.

On the morning of postoperative day No. 2, she had a cardiac
arrest.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  Ischemic colitis and enteritis.
2.  Metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma with malnutrition,
    ascites.
3.  Pyuria.
3.  Sepsis and shock.
4.  Cardiac arrest and death.

 hematoma.

 duct are identified within the pancreatic body and tail, with small areas of

 duct cannot be confirmed on this study.

ADDENDUM:

After initially preparing the patient for rehabilitation as
indicated in the first part of this discharge summary, it was
decided to keep the patient for further monitoring.

were held for about four days, her creatinine returned to
baseline but she was found somnolent in the morning.
Arterial blood gases revealed a pH of about 7.2, pCO2 144 and
pO2 of 45.  The patient was started on BiPAP and was
diuresed.  She turned around within 24 hours and was returned
back to the floor.  She had been transferred briefly to the
unit so that she could be maintained on BiPAP.  After
returning to the floor, her mental status continued to wax
and wane likely secondary to depression.  She can become
nearly unresponsive with her bouts of depression and can be
easily confused for hypercarbia.  The patient was eventually
stabilized on a diuretic regimen of 2 mg p.o. once daily of
Bumex.  Her creatinine remained stable on this regimen and
she had no further episodes of unresponsiveness due to
hypercarbia.  Her ace inhibitor continues to be held because
her blood pressure is normal and we do not want to further
insult her kidneys given that her creatinine tends to rise
quite easily with diuresis.

Pulmonary consultation was called during this patient's
hospitalization and they became quite involved in her care.
They were able to offer the following evaluation of her
pulmonary status:  She has a primary respiratory acidosis
with a primary metabolic alkalosis and a compensatory
metabolic alkalosis.  Her primary respiratory acidosis is
primarily secondary to her severe emphysema which increases
her work of breathing as well as bilateral pleural effusions
which further increase her work of breathing.  Also, her
increased pCO2 is secondary to decreased respiratory drive
which is due in part to hyperoxia. A pO2 greater than 65 and
an oxygen saturation of greater than 93% would be probably
the best to hope for in this patient without causing a
further decrease in her respiratory drive.  Diuresis of this
patient has also created a primary metabolic alkalosis which
permits her pH to increase such that her drive to breathe is
further decreased which further exacerbates increased pCO2.
It should be noted that this patient is a chronic CO2
retained with a baseline CO2 in the low 40s.  Her CO2 did
rise to 52 during this hospitalization for the above
mentioned reasons.  Also for the above mentioned reasons, it
is thought that too much supplementary oxygen may dangerously
increase her pCO2.  Oxygen supplementation of one to two
liters by nasal cannula should permit adequate oxygenation of
mental status while she is awake.  It was also suggested by
pulmonary that her target potassium be 5.0 in order to
decrease her alkalosis.  They also recommended increasing her
dose of Flovent to four puffs twice a day.

Psychiatry also saw the patient in house given that she has
not had any psychiatric follow-up presumably since her
hospitalization in the psychiatric geriatric unit.  Her
waxing and [**Doctor Last Name 688**] mental status is presumed secondary to
depression which she has been diagnosed with in the past.
The patient can become confused with hypercarbia which
closely mimics her decreased responsiveness with
exacerbations of her depression.  Psychiatry felt that the
patient was doing well on her current regimen of Celexa and
Zyprexa and recommended discontinuing Ativan and Ambien.
This was done while the patient was in house.  They also
recommend psychiatric follow-up while the patient is
hospitalized at rehabilitation and suggested the patient's
family consider an option such as [**Doctor First Name 1191**] Day Hospital if and
when the patient ultimately makes it back home.  Again, this
patient does need psychiatric follow-up while she is in
rehabilitation.

The patient is a very big fall risk.  She fell about four
times while in house but managed to avoid injury.  At the
time of discharge, she has no neurological deficits and is
alert and oriented and is mentating well.  She did sustain
several skin tears during her falls much in part due to
attempts to hold her up.  Her skin is very brittle and it
tears very easily.  She was seen by a skin care nurse and
appropriate care of her skin tears was taken.

The patient was also transfused with packed red blood cells
to maintain her hematocrit greater than 28.0.  She was
continued on Digoxin for her atrial fibrillation.  Despite
her falls, she was also continued on low dose Coumadin 2 mg
p.o. q.h.s. to maintain an INR of 1.5 to 2.0 given recent
evidence that this range of INR can be effective for
preventing stroke in atrial fibrillation patients while
decreasing the risk of bleeding if they are a fall risk.  Her
ace inhibitor is being held due to her tenuous renal function
with diuresis.

48-year-old woman with a history of end-stage renal disease
(on hemodialysis), hypothyroidism, seizure disorder, and a
history of migraine headaches who presented to the Emergency
Department with complaints of a severe headache for several
days.

Her headache began two days prior, with a sudden onset,
preceded by spots in front of her eyes.  On the day prior to
admission, she continued to have a headache at dialysis.
After dialysis, she vomited at home and subsequently had a
tonic-clonic seizure which was witnessed.

She presented to the Emergency Department where she had a
repeat tonic-clonic seizure lasting two to three minutes.
She received intravenous Ativan and a Dilantin load.  Her
systolic blood pressure was noted to be greater than 200.
She was ultimately placed on a nitroprusside drip in the
Emergency Department for control.  This resulted in a
resolution of the majority of her headache.

A computed tomography of the head and a lumbar puncture were
negative.  The patient was admitted to the Medical Intensive
Care Unit for hypertensive urgency.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1.  End-stage renal disease (on hemodialysis for the past
five years).
2.  Hypothyroidism.
3.  Seizure disorder.
4.  Low back pain (chronic).
5.  Status post right partial colectomy secondary to
intussusception.
6.  Status post small-bowel obstruction.
7.  Status post cholecystectomy.
8.  Migraine headaches.

ALLERGIES:  No known drug allergies.

MEDICATIONS ON ADMISSION: (To the Intensive Care Unit)
1.  Fentanyl and labetalol drips.
2.  Zestril 10 mg by mouth twice per day.
3.  Synthroid 125 mcg by mouth once per day.
4.  Dilantin 300 mg by mouth once per day.
5.  Percocet by mouth as needed.
6.  Renagel 800 mg by mouth three times per day.
7.  Extra-Strength Tums four tablets three times per day.
8.  Soma.

SOCIAL HISTORY:  She is an ex-smoker.  No alcohol.  She is a
teacher.  She is married.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION ON PRESENTATION:  On admission her vital
signs revealed a temperature of 97 degrees Fahrenheit, her
blood pressure was 161/79, her heart rate was 82, her
respiratory rate was 14, and her oxygen saturation was 100%
on room air.  In general, she was an uncomfortable
African-American woman moving in bed in distress.  The pupils
were equal, round, and reactive to light and accommodation.
The extraocular muscles were intact.  There was no
photophobia.  The oral mucosa were moist.  The oropharynx was
clear.  The pupils were 1 mm.  Her heart rate and rhythm were
regular with a 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the left
sternal border.  Normal first heart sounds and second heart
sounds.  The lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally.
The abdomen was obese, soft, nontender, and nondistended.
The extremities were warm and dry without edema.
Neurologically, cranial nerves II through XII were intact.
She was alert and interactive.

PERTINENT LABORATORY VALUES ON PRESENTATION:  White blood
cell count was 7.2, her hematocrit was 36.6, and her
platelets were 157.  Chemistry-7 was significant for a blood
urea nitrogen of 31 and a creatinine of 7.4.  She had a
phenytoin level of 2.9.

PERTINENT RADIOLOGY/IMAGING:  A computed tomography of the
head showed no bleed and no mass.

BRIEF SUMMARY OF HOSPITAL COURSE:  After admission to the
Intensive Care Unit, her blood pressure was controlled with
intravenous labetalol, and she was weaned off the intravenous
nitroprusside.

Over the next 48 hours she was transitioned again to oral
intake, and her lisinopril was bumped up to better control
her blood pressure.  She had no recurrent episodes of
hypertension while hospitalized.

She was reloaded on her phenytoin.  The levels were checked
and were in the therapeutic range.  Throughout the remainder
of her hospitalization, she had no further seizure activity.
She was followed by the Neurology Service in consultation
while in house.

Her headaches improved shortly after admission with a dose of
metoclopramide.  It was believed that these actually did
represent true migraine headaches; although, they may have
also been related to her hypertensive urgency.

She was discharged to the floor in stable condition and from
the floor was discharged to home.  She was to follow up with
her regular nephrologist and with Neurology.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  End-stage renal disease (on hemodialysis).
2.  Hypertensive urgency.
3.  Chronic hypertension.
4.  Migraine headache.

DISCHARGE STATUS:  Discharge status was to home.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:  Condition on discharge was good.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS/FOLLOWUP:  The patient was instructed
to follow up with her regular nephrologist (Dr. [**First Name4 (NamePattern1) **] [**Last Name (NamePattern1) 174**])
and with her primary care physician.

anterior resection, colostomy closure, incisional hernia
repair x2 with component separation.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  Patient is a 79-year-old woman
with a history of hypertension, who three years ago underwent
an emergency operation for a perforated diverticulitis
resulting in an end colostomy and Hartmann's pouch.  She was
interested in having her colostomy closed as well as having
two incisional hernias repair, one at the site of her midline
incision, and one at the site of her left lower quadrant
around her colostomy.

CONCISE SUMMARY OF HOSPITAL COURSE:  The patient was taken to
the operating room as planned on [**2122-11-2**] for
colostomy closure, incisional hernia repair x2 with component
separation.  The operation was without any complications.

On postoperative day 0, the patient had issues with low urine
output and received multiple fluid boluses to maintain
adequate urine output.  Additionally, it was noted that the
patient had intraoperative bradycardia as well as ectopy,
cardiac laboratories were sent and found to be within normal
limits.  Her CKs were elevated postsurgically, but she had a
normal MB fraction and troponin.  An epidural catheter was
left in place, the patient had two JPs draining
serosanguinous fluid, and she left the OR and PACU, and was
transferred to the floor requiring O2 at 6 liters nasal
cannula.

A review of her in's and out's on the first day of her
hospital course showed that she received 5.2 liters in the
OR, PACU, and floor, and put out 510 cc of urine output.  On
postoperative day #1, urine culture was sent and later
revealed Klebsiella that was pansensitive, for which she was
started on levofloxacin.  That night, the night float
resident was called as the patient was found to be
desaturating to 89% on 5 liters nasal cannula, and at this
time, she was also complaining of shortness of breath and
some persistent abdominal pain.  An arterial blood gas was
obtained revealing a pH of 7.31, pCO2 of 53, pO2 of 50,
bicarb of 26, and base deficit of -1.  The chest x-ray
revealed a right pleural effusion as well as a CHF-like
pattern.

Based on this blood gas and the patient's deteriorating
respiratory status, she was transferred to the ICU for closer
monitoring, she was given 20 mg of IV Lasix for diuresis, and
she was put on a nonrebreather and found to be sating
improved at 96%.  An art line was placed in the ICU.

On postoperative day #2, repeat blood gas showed a pH of
7.33, pCO2 of 54, pO2 of 53, and a bicarb of 30 on 70% O2.
Later that day she was found once again to be tachypneic with
desats to 85% on 100% nonrebreather as well as hypertensive
to the 180s systolic.  The decision was made to intubate the
patient in the ICU, which was accomplished without
difficulty.  A right internal jugular central venous line was
placed.  At this time, the patient was bronched revealing a
large amount of thick secretions that were sent for culture
later revealing a moderate amount of yeast.

Her epidural was continued at this time, and she was
continued to be diuresed.  A search for the cause of her
desaturations was made, and an echocardiogram was obtained
revealing an abnormality of the septal motion and pattern of
the right ventricle as well as mild left atrial dilatation,
but was otherwise normal revealing normal left ventricular
function with an EF greater than 55%.

A CT angiogram was performed that was negative for pulmonary
embolus, however, was significant for opacification
bilaterally of her lower lobes as well as right upper lobe
consolidation that was consistent with a pneumonia.

The patient, on postoperative day three, was switched from
Levaquin to Zosyn to cover her UTI and pneumonia.  On
postoperative day three, she was noted to have several PAC's
with ectopy on the monitor with an EKG revealing atrial
fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response, as well as a
left bundle branch block.  She was rate controlled on
Lopressor and diltiazem with adequate response.

On postoperative day #4, the results from the bronchial
washings came back and the patient was started on
fluconazole.  At this time, her epidural was D/C'd, and a
nasogastric tube was inserted to start tube feeds.

On postoperative day six, the patient continued to have
ectopy overnight and had failed CPAP, and therefore remained
intubated.  However, she was tolerating tube feeds well.  A
cardiac consultation was obtained on the basis of her ectopy
and their assessment revealed that her rhythm was consistent
with episodes of atrial fibrillation with superimposed rate
dependent left bundle branch block, with no evidence of
ventricular tachycardia.  They recommended to continue her
beta blockade at a reduced dosage of 5 mg IV q.4h.
Cardiology did not recommend Coumadin at this time.  Patient
was additionally transfused 1 unit of packed red blood cells
for a hematocrit of 27.5 which improved to 30.8 status post
transfusion.  That night, the patient spiked to a temperature
of 101.0, however, a workup of blood cultures, urine
cultures, and changing the central venous line was negative.

On postoperative day #7, pulmonary toilet was continued.
Tube feeds were continued at goal and the patient was
continued to diurese on Lasix.  Her ventilator parameters
were weaned on postoperative day eight, and she continued to
have white secretions from her tube, but was otherwise
tolerating intubation well and mouthing words to her family.
There were no new events on postoperative days nine or 10.

On postoperative day 11, the patient was successfully
extubated, and at this time, was also evaluated by Physical
Therapy.  Her midline wound was found to be tender, hard, as
well as mildly erythematous stretch of 2.5 cm.  Staples were
removed revealing a midline hematoma, but did not require
drainage.  The wound was then packed with wet-to-dry
dressings that were changed on a t.i.d. basis.

On postoperative day #12, the patient was transferred to the
floor after a chest x-ray revealed improved right upper lobe
aeration and improving consolidation in the lower lobes, but
significant for persistent bibasilar consolidations.  The
patient did tolerate a regular diet and was transferred to
the floor on 95% 4 liters nasal cannula.  Her nasogastric
tube was D/C'd at this time.

On postoperative day 13, the patient's p.o. intake increased.
She was ambulating well with Physical Therapy and her Foley
was D/C'd that night.  The wound care was continued
wet-to-dry dressings t.i.d.

On postoperative day 14, Physical Therapy continued to
ambulate the patient and she was found to be sating
adequately at 92% on room air while ambulating and she was
determined to be safe for home disposition.  Her right
internal jugular veins central venous line was D/C'd at this
time, and the patient was encouraged to increase her p.o.
intake.  She was sent home this day on postoperative day 14
with services for wet-to-dry dressing changes b.i.d., home
Physical Therapy, and checks of her O2 saturation by visiting
nurses.  Her principal care provider was called and notified
that we had started her on albuterol, Atrovent treatment
which were improving her lung examination, and he agreed with
sending her home on a lower dose of p.o. metoprolol 12.5
t.i.d. for heart function.

CONDITION ON DISCHARGE:  Stable.

DISCHARGE STATUS:  Home with services.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
1. Percocet 1-2 tablets p.o. q.4-6h. prn pain.
2. Atrovent inhaler 18 mcg two puffs q.i.d. for two weeks.
3. Albuterol MDI 90 mcg container:  two puffs q.4-6h. prn
shortness of breath or wheezing.
4. Nystatin swish and swallow 5 cc orally q.i.d.
5. Famotidine 20 mg one tablet p.o. b.i.d.
6. Metoprolol 50 mg tablet:  [**2-7**] of a tablet p.o. b.i.d.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:  Resume a regular diet.  Activity:
No heavy lifting or straining for two weeks until the midline
abdominal wound heals.  The patient was instructed to call
her physician or return to the Emergency Department if she
developed any fever or chills, temperature greater than
101.5, shortness of breath or difficulty breathing, drainage
or bleeding from the wound, or unable to eat or drink.

FOLLOW-UP PLANS:
1. The patient was instructed to contact Dr.[**Name (NI) 10946**]
office to arrange a follow-up appointment to be seen within
1-2 weeks.
2. The patient was instructed to followup with her primary
care physician, [**Last Name (NamePattern4) **]. [**Last Name (STitle) 51525**] within one week.
3. Additionally, the patient was setup with VNA services for
wet-to-dry dressing changes b.i.d. for midline abdominal
wound as well as home PT.  The patient will have her O2
saturations checked by visiting nurses and if found to be
less than 88%, she will be placed on home O2 to be followed
up by her primary care provider.

These discharge plans were discussed with the attending.

 increased uptake are likely secondary to postoperative changes.  A focal area of
 uptake is present in the right posterior lung paraspinal region.  There is some
 corresponding irregularity of the lung tissue in this region.  This focal
 avidity is also likely secondary to postoperative changes.

 corresponds to an adrenal mass, which measures approximately 2.5 x 3 cm.  The
 SUV of this lesion is 12.5.  In comparison to prior chest CT of [**2166-10-31**], there
 has been marked interval increase in size of this left adrenal mass.

 pericardial region, all consistent with postoperative change.  2) Focal area of
 increased avidity in the right posterior lung paraspinal region, which is also
 likely postoperative in nature.  3) Left adrenal mass with high FDG avidity,
 highly suspicious for metastatic disease.

receive any intervention for intracranial hemorrhage
throughout her hospital stay.  She had a follow-up head
computed tomography which showed a resolving subarachnoid
hemorrhage, one resolving subdural hemorrhage, with some
persistent subdural hemorrhage that had not grown in size.

Neurosurgery had been following the patient and felt that the
patient's intracranial hemorrhage was stable, and no further
intervention was needed.

Throughout her hospital course, the patient gradually
improved.  Her mental status improved, and the patient began
to move all extremities with increasing strength.  She was
alert and oriented by head movements and would speak on
occasion.

Physical Therapy, and Occupational Therapy, and Speech
Therapy were consulted to work with the patient.  She
remained selectively nonverbal throughout her hospital
course; however, she was fully able to answer questions
through nonverbal gestures.

Intensive Care Unit.  At that time, she had been placed on

slowly decreased her oxygen requirement and began to have
oxygen saturations on room air.  After receiving

discontinued for a finished course of pneumonia.  A follow-up
chest x-ray was ordered which showed a stable left pleural

improved examination.

central line infection.  She had one temperature spike on

coagulase-negative Staphylococcus which was sensitive to
vancomycin.  At that time, vancomycin was added to her
regimen.  She remained afebrile throughout the rest of her
hospital course.  After the addition of vancomycin, repeat
blood cultures remained negative.  She had a peripherally
inserted central catheter line placed to finish a 14-day
course of vancomycin for line sepsis.

course.

count.  A search was done to look for additional infectious
causes, and stool cultures were sent to look for Clostridium
difficile (which was negative), and follow-up blood cultures
were also negative.  Abdominal laboratories were drawn showed
no evidence of intra-abdominal process or infection.  The
patient continued to remain afebrile.  The cause of the
patient's white blood cell count was unknown, but was thought
to in part be related to central nervous system effect from
her intracranial hemorrhage.  The patient continued her seven
days of vancomycin for her line sepsis and was to have
follow-up laboratories drawn as an outpatient.

her transfer to the Medicine Service with episodes of heart
rates up to 140.  At times she was found to be increasingly
irregular but not found to be in atrial fibrillation.  Her
metoprolol was increased up to 100 mg by mouth three times
per day.  Cardiology was involved to work up this
tachycardia.  The patient had also been given fluid boluses
with a modest decrease in her heart rate.

patient likely had multifocal atrial tachycardia and that it
did not appear that she had atrial fibrillation at that time.

60 mg by mouth four times per day with much improved decrease
in her heart rates.  Her lisinopril was decreased to 20 mg by
mouth once per day to avoid any decrease in blood pressures.

ventricular tachycardia but maintained stable vital signs.
Electrolytes were repleted.  Because the patient had normal
cardiac function from a previous echocardiogram, no further
management was indicated at that time.

placed on tube feeds in the Neurosurgery Intensive Care Unit.

evaluation showed that the patient was safe to have soft diet
without risk of aspiration pneumonia.  It was felt that her

oral diet well.

anemia of chronic disease.  There was no evidence of blood
loss.  The patient's hematocrit remained stable throughout

stabilized and her care could be continued at outpatient
rehabilitation with proper physical therapy, occupational
therapy, and speech therapy.

CONDITION AT DISCHARGE:

DISCHARGE STATUS:  Discharge status was to an extended care

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  Subarachnoid hemorrhage/subdural bleed.
2.  Aspiration pneumonia.
3.  Line sepsis.
4.  Multifocal atrial tachycardia.

1.  Heparin 5000 units subcutaneously q.12h. (to be continued

2.  Lansoprazole 30-mg tablets one tablet by mouth once per
day.
3.  Metoprolol 100-mg tablets one tablet by mouth three times
per day.
4.  Miconazole powder as needed (for perirectal irritation).
5.  Diltiazem 60-mg tablets one tablet by mouth four times
per day.
6.  Lisinopril 20-mg tablets one tablet by mouth once per
day.
7.  Vancomycin 1 g intravenously q.12h. (for 7 days for a
total of a 14-day course).
8.  Tylenol by mouth as needed (for pain/fever).
9.  Ipratropium nebulizers q.6h. as needed (for shortness of
breath or wheezing).

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS/FOLLOWUP:
1.  The patient was instructed to follow up with her primary
care physician within one to two weeks after discharge.
2.  The patient was also instructed to follow up as an
outpatient with Neurosurgery for an outpatient evaluation of
resolving subarachnoid hemorrhage and subdural bleed in 2 weeks
with a repeat Head CT
3.  The patient was instructed that if she had any further

symptoms that she should immediately contact her primary care
physician and return to the Emergency Department.

 vertebral artery.  At this point, evaluation of the above with injection of
 contrast and biplane angiography as well as two-dimensional rotational

 fistula.  Injection of the right subclavian artery reveals no evidence of
 significant stenosis or dissection.  Injection of the right vertebral artery
 reveals a somewhat tortuous course with no evidence of significant stenosis or
 dissection and a smaller caliber on the right than on the left vertebral
 artery.  Injection of the intracranial portion reveals no evidence of

 anteroinferior cerebellar artery.  Injection of the left subclavian artery
 reveals no evidence of significant stenosis or dissection.  Injection of the
 left vertebral artery reveals it to be tortuous in the cervical portion but
 reveals no evidence of significant stenosis or dissection.  It is the dominant
 of the two.  Injection of the left external carotid artery reveals no evidence
 of stenosis or dissection and no abnormal arteriovenous shunting.  Injection
 of the left internal carotid artery reveals the presence of a 12 x 7 mm
 posterior communicating artery aneurysm with a 6-mm neck.  In addition, the
 course of the supraclinoid segment around the siphon in the cavernous segment
 is irregular and has characteristics of an intracranial atherosclerosis which
 is not hemodynamically significant.  Following the deployment of the coils,
 there is excellent embolization of the aneurysm with no filling of the dome
 portion of the aneurysm and a small amount of loose packing at the proximal
 neck owing to the wide neck of the aneurysm.

   Her husband and brother have been very involved in her care. Her
   brother returned to [**Name (NI) 652**] yesterday and will return on Thursday for
   another family meeting/decision on goals of care.

nontender and nondistended and the extremities were without
clubbing, cyanosis or edema.  The patient had normal rectal
tone per examination and the patient was guaiac negative.

25.0, platelet count of 207.  Electrolytes drawn at the time
were within normal limits.  A CT scan of the thoracic spine
revealed a T9 and T10 compression fracture as well as a
fracture of the spinous process at T9.  A T12 transverse
process fracture and mild canal narrowing at the levels of
T11 and T12.

At the time of admission the orthopedic spine service was
consulted and their recommendation was for reexamination
following lightening of sedation for a full neurological
examination.  Pending the patient's intubated and sedated
status they recommended maintenance with a log roll
precautions at all times.  After initial workup in the trauma
bay the patient was transferred to the Trauma Intensive Care
Unit where repeat laboratories were significant for a
hematocrit of 33, white blood cell count of 16.3 and a
platelet count of 161.  In addition to the plan outlined by
the orthopedics spine consult the Trauma Intensive Care Unit
team pursued a bronchoscopy for diminished right upper lobe
breath sounds as well as a left shoulder plain film to assess
for acute trauma.  Additional radiological workup was
significant for a left pneumothorax being treated with a left
chest tube and multiple left rib fractures.  Head CT,
abdominal CT and diagnostic peritoneal lavage were all
negative.  Upon repeat chest x-ray the patient was found to
also have a right pleural effusion and this was treated on
hospital day two with a placement of a right chest tube.  The
output from this chest tube was immediately 50 cc of
sanguinous fluid and after the tube was placed to suction an
additional 20 cc of sanguinous fluid was drawn from the chest
tube.

On follow up consultation orthopedics recommended a [**Doctor Last Name **]
brace for treatment of the patient's compression fractures
and other spinal fractures.  This brace was fitted to the
patient on hospital day two, [**2184-2-2**].  On hospital
day three the patient continued to be intubated and sedated.

have coarse breath sounds bilaterally.  The plan per the
Intensive Care Unit team was to wean to extubation and to
hold sedation after fitting of the TLSO brace.  The patient
was also placed on a CIWA protocol, benzodiazepines for
treatment of his incipient alcohol withdraw.  On [**2184-2-5**] cultures were returned on the patient's bronchoalveolar
lavage, which was performed on [**2184-2-2**].  These
tests were positive for Methacillin resistant staph aureus
and the patient was placed on Vancomycin.  On [**2184-2-6**] the Neurology Service was consulted to evaluate the
patient's mental status, which had still not returned to
baseline despite the weaning of sedation.  Their assessment
was that this otherwise healthy 32 year-old male had an
altered mentals status probably due to the factor of
medications subsequent to high doses of benzodiazepines and
morphine.  Increased right leg weakness and decreased
sensation to the right lower extremity were attributed to his
known thoracic spine fractures.

To further workup these neurological deficits the Neurology
Service recommended an MRI of the full spinal cord to
evaluate for nerve root or spinal cord injury.  They also
recommended a speech and swallow evaluation for this patient
as well as weaning of all sedation to allow this patient's
mental status to normalize.  These recommendations were
followed by the Trauma Intensive Care Unit team.  On [**2184-2-8**] the patient had blood cultures and urine cultures
drawn pursuant to recommendations by the Neurology Service
for a workup of his recurrent fevers.  In addition,
electroencephalogram was performed as well as a MRI of the
brain with diffusion weighted imaging was ordered to evaluate
the patient for diffuse axonal injury.  Final read on the MRI
of the spinal canal was obtained on [**2184-2-9**] and
this showed cord compression and fracture collapse and
worsening fracture.  Given these findings the Orthopedic
Service assessment was that the [**Doctor Last Name **] brace was not adequate
treatment and a full body TLSO brace was fitted.  To provide
stabilization for this patient's spinal fractures, the
patient was taken to the Operating Room by Orthopedics on
[**2184-2-10**] for posterior stabilization of his
compression fracture.  The patient underwent a T7 through T12
laminectomy and fusion done by the Orthopedic Spine Service
on [**2184-2-10**].  This procedure was completed without
complications.  Postoperatively, the patient initially showed
minimal movement of his right arm and left leg to pain,
however, these initial neurological changes on examination
resolved subsequently and were not suggestive of
intraoperative cord trauma.  On postoperative day two the
patient was intubated and sedated and continued to have low
grade fevers with a T max of 101.5. He was moving all
extremities spontaneously and able to squeeze the examiner's
fingers on command.

continued on Vancomycin and Levaquin.  On [**2184-2-12**]

swallow examination was scheduled to evaluate the patient for
initiating oral intake.  As far as his mental status the
patient continued to be confused and was talking repeatedly
and perseverating over topics especially involving his former
occupation as a food delivery person.  On [**2184-2-16**] a
bedside swallow evaluation was performed with recommendations
to continue the patient NPO with an nasogastric tube and to
obtain a video swallow study to rule out aspiration.  This
was pursuant to observations by the bedside swallow evaluator
of overt speech and swallow aspiration on large straw sips of
water.  This video swallow study was performed later on
[**2184-2-16**] and the results of the study were moderate
to severe oropharyngeal dysphagia were observed by piece meal

injury given his quite severe roll over motor vehicle
accident.  An ENT consult was obtained to evaluate the
